title: The Value of Self-esteem

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Gauging the value of self-esteem requires, first of all, a sensible way to measure it. Most investigators ask people what they think of themselves. Naturally enough, the answers are often coloured by the common tendency to want to make oneself look good. Unfortunately, psychologists lack any better method to judge self-esteem, which is worrisome because similar self-ratings of other attributes often prove to be way off.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Consider, for instance, the relation between self-esteem and physical attractiveness. Several studies have explored correlations between these qualities, generally finding clear positive links when people rate themselves on both properties. It seems plausible that physically attractive people would end up with high self-esteem because they may be treated more favourably than unattractive ones – being more popular, more sought after and so forth. But it could well be that those who score highly on self-esteem scales by claiming to be wonderful people all around also boast of being physically attractive.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In 1995 Edward F. Diener and Brian Wolsic of the University of Illinois were involved in research to examine this possibility. They obtained self-esteem scores from a broad sample of the population and then photographed everybody, presenting these pictures to a panel of judges, who evaluated the subjects for their attractiveness. Ratings based on full-length photographs showed no significant correlation with self-esteem. Head-and-shoulders close-ups fared slightly better, but even this finding is dubious, because individuals with high self-esteem might take particular care to present themselves well by wearing jewellery and attractive clothing. The 1995 study suggests as much: when the judges were shown pictures of just the participants’ unadorned faces, the modest correlation between attractiveness and self-esteem fell to zero. In that same investigation, however, self-reported physical attractiveness was found to have as trong correlation with self-esteem.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Another issue to be considered when looking at self-esteem is the effect of self-esteemon behaviour. The question of causality goes to the heart of the debate. If high self-esteem brings about positive outcomes then it may well be worth the effort of trying to cultivate this feeling. But if the correlations mean simply that a positive self-image is a result of success or good behaviour, there is little to be gained by raising self-esteem alone.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Early work in this area showed positive correlations between self-esteem and academic performance in schools but modern studies have cast doubt on this claim. Such inferences about causality are possible when subjects are examined at two different times. In 1986, Sheila M. Pottebaum, Timothy Z. Keithand Stewart W. Ehly tested more than 23,000 high school students, first in the 10th grade and then again in the 12th grade. They found that self-esteem in the 10th grade is only weakly predictive of academic achievement in the 12th grade. Academic achievement in the 10th grade correlates with self-esteem in the 12th grade only slightly better. Such results, which are now available from multiple studies, certainly do not indicate that raising self-esteem offers students much benefit. Studies of possible links between workers’ self-regard and job performance echo what has been found within schools: there is no strong link between occupational success and good self-image.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The failure to contribute significantly at school or at the office would easily be offset if a heightened sense of self-worth helped someone to get along better with others. Having a good self-image might make someone more likeable in so far as people prefer to associate with confident, positive individuals and generally avoid those who suffer from self-doubt and insecurities. People who regard themselves highly generally state that they are popular and rate their friendships as being of superior quality to those described by people with low self-esteem, who report more negative interactions and less social support. But as Julia Bishop and Heidi M. Inderbitzen-Nolan of the University of Nebraska-Lincoln showed in 1995, these assertions do not reflect reality. The investigators asked 542 ninth-grade students to nominate their most-liked and least-liked in their year group, and the resulting rankings displayed no correlation whatsoever with self-esteem scores.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The consistent finding is that people with high self-esteem are significantly happier than others. They are also less likely to be depressed. In one especially compelling study, published in 1995, more than 13,000 college students were surveyed, and high self-esteem emerged as the strongest factor in overall life satisfaction. In 2004 Lyubomirsky, Tkach and Dimatteo of the University of California reported data from more than 600 adults ranging in age from 51 to 95. Once again, happiness and self-esteem proved to be closely tied. Before it is safe to conclude that high self-esteem leads to happiness, however, further research must address the shortcomings of the work that has been done so far.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: First, causation needs to be established. It seems possible that high self-esteem brings about happiness, but no research has shown this outcome. It is plausible that occupational, academic or interpersonal success cause both happiness and high self-esteem. Second it must be recognised that happiness has been studied mainly by means of self-report, and the tendency of some people towards negativity may produce both their own opinions of themselves and unfavourable evaluations of other aspects of their life. Clearly, objective measures of happiness are going to be difficult, if not impossible, to obtain, but that does not mean that self-reports should be accepted uncritically.

subtitle: People intuitively recognise the importance of high self-esteem (having a favourable opinion of themselves) to their psychological health. So it isn’t particularly remarkable that most of us try to protect it and enhance it in ourselves whenever possible
